title: AppBot exec console-binding constitution: fated to its own console
desc: Constitutional law for wkappbot exec and every process-touching command: bind only to the console you can prove you own, corroborate with a second axis, fail closed on ambiguity, defend out-of-console reach in layers, rank own-console then own-descendants first with taskkill above all, and adopt a shortcut-launched repo daemon by its published claim rather than by a CWD guess.
steps: DECISION: THE CONSTITUTION IN ONE LINE -- wkappbot exec is FATED TO ITS OWN CONSOLE. It may drive only the console it can prove it owns, and it must surrender the input side rather than reach into a console belonging to someone else. WHEN: any change to exec transport, keystroke delivery, reply rules, console binding, or partner-process resolution. HOW: run wkappbot skill read wkexec-conpty-keystrokes-ladder for the transport contract, then apply the Articles below IN ORDER, refusing at the first article that cannot be satisfied. WHY: the owner named this law on 2026-08-20 after his own typing kept vanishing while the installed agy ran under exec, and after exec input reached unrelated windows -- to the human at that keyboard, a process typing into a console it does not own is indistinguishable from something hostile.

DECISION: ARTICLE 1 -- THE CONSOLE IS THE IDENTITY AND THE WORKING FOLDER IS NOT. exec must NEVER select its partner process by current working directory, and a CWD match alone must never bind anything. WHEN: resolving which process, console, or window an exec invocation belongs to. HOW: resolve the attached console first via GetConsoleWindow and GetConsoleProcessList, and run wkappbot skill read standard-appbot-window for the ancestor-walk contract that already governs caller-HWND resolution here. WHY: Claude Code, wkchat, agy and codex all run with the same repo root as their CWD, so a CWD match selects a stranger with high probability; this repo has already lost a session-identity resolution to exactly this mistake, which is why session identity is now resolved by exact file path and never by a CWD scan.

DECISION: ARTICLE 2 -- PROVE OWNERSHIP BEFORE TAKING THE INPUT SIDE. Before any input-side action, meaning a console read with intercept, a key injection, or a console-input-record write, exec must establish that it is the owning client of that console rather than a guest on it. WHEN: immediately before starting any reader thread or any injector that touches console input. HOW: call GetConsoleProcessList and compare the attached PID set against the expected set of self plus the spawned child, and run wkappbot skill read mystery-window-diagnosis whenever that set contains anything unexplained. WHY: the console input buffer is a SHARED resource with no arbitration, and a read with intercept CONSUMES the keystroke so no other attached client ever sees it -- which is precisely how the owner keystrokes disappeared while exec was running.

DECISION: ARTICLE 3 -- TWO AXES MUST AGREE AND THE THIRD MAY ONLY NARROW. Binding requires the console axis AND one corroborating axis, never any single axis alone. The three axes are console, session-identity, and working folder; the working folder is admissible ONLY to disambiguate among candidates already selected by console, and never to select one. WHEN: choosing the partner process for an exec invocation. HOW: treat the console axis as mandatory, corroborate with session identity, and run wkappbot skill read eye-ipc-caller-hwnd-resolution for how this repo already ranks such evidence. WHY: the owner first proposed matching on ANY ONE of the three axes, and that shape is the defect rather than the fix -- each axis fails in a different way, so a rule satisfiable by one axis is only as strong as its weakest axis.

DECISION: ARTICLE 3B -- THE EMBEDDED-HOST CLAUSE, COVERING VS CODE AND EVERY OTHER EXTENSION HOST. Inside VS Code, a JetBrains IDE, or any extension host, the OS parent chain is NOT a usable axis and must not be treated as one. WHEN: exec runs anywhere the caller was launched by an extension host or through a detached spawn. HOW: substitute session-identity environment evidence for the parent chain by reading CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT, VSCODE_PID, WT_SESSION and CODEX_HOME, and run wkappbot skill read concurrent-ai-isolation-env-var-detection-beats-parent-chain for the measured precedence order. WHY: AppBotPipe.Spawn uses DETACHED_PROCESS, which severs the Windows parent chain by design so the parent reports as an unrelated low PID, and five live daemons measured on 2026-08-20 had no parent at all, meaning the axis fails open exactly when it is most needed. A second hazard belongs only to this clause: a VS Code integrated terminal is ITSELF a pseudo-console shared across the whole terminal tab, so a console reader started inside it steals from the host tab rather than from a private console.

DECISION: ARTICLE 4 -- AMBIGUITY MEANS RENDER-ONLY, NEVER A GUESS. If the Articles above do not yield exactly one partner, exec must decline the input side, continue in render-only mode, and print one line naming which article failed and what it saw. WHEN: any binding attempt ending with zero candidates or with more than one. HOW: fail closed and emit the reason, and run wkappbot skill read harness-guard-exemption-ladder-spec for the fail-closed posture this harness already requires of its own gates. WHY: silently typing into the wrong window is strictly worse than not typing at all, because the wrong-window case is invisible to the operator and corrupts state nobody will associate with exec -- a refusal costs one visible round, a wrong guess costs every round built on top of it.

DECISION: ARTICLE 5 -- HUMAN PRESENCE IS MEASURED, NOT INFERRED FROM A FLAG, AND THE SHARED INPUT PIPE MUST BE ARBITRATED. CORRECTED THE SAME DAY IT WAS WRITTEN, 2026-08-20, after the owner pointed out that a rule which grows too broad is itself the defect: the first draft said any drive-the-child flag proves no human is present, and that is FALSE for reply. A reply rule is REACTIVE and composes with a live human -- the owner types to agy himself while the rules auto-dismiss its approval prompts, so both are true at once, and switching off the console reader would have taken his keyboard away entirely. The correct split is by EVIDENCE, not by flag: keystrokes-file and onexit are fully scripted and do prove absence, while reply proves nothing about presence and must never be read that way. Presence is measured from the console itself, whether input is redirected and whether a console is attached at all. AND THE REAL HAZARD IS ARBITRATION: a reply firing mid-keystroke interleaves its bytes with relayed human bytes on the ONE ConPTY input pipe, which corrupts the line the human was typing -- that is the mechanism behind input not getting through, not the mere existence of the reader. So a reply must take the pipe exclusively for the duration of its sequence, and the presence test must live in ONE place that every transport reads. WHEN: adding a delivery flag, or touching any condition that decides whether a console reader starts. HOW: hoist the single predicate instead of restating it per transport, and run wkappbot skill read verify-tool-or-guard-synthetic-live-static-howto to prove the reader really did not start rather than reading the condition and believing it. WHY: this Article exists because the twin predicates had ALREADY drifted -- RunCommand.cs line 260 defined the correct three-way condition including reply rules, while RunCommand.Pty.cs line 206 passed a narrower two-way condition omitting them, so the ConPTY path started the key-stealing reader for exactly the force-pty plus reply combination the installed agy uses.

DECISION: ARTICLE 6 -- THE BINDING DIES WITH THE SESSION. When the child has exited, or the console owner is gone, or the console handle is no longer valid, exec must exit rather than keep polling; no reader may outlive the thing it was reading for. WHEN: writing any loop that polls console input, and every teardown path. HOW: tie reader lifetime to the child handle and to console validity, and run wkappbot skill read core-worker-logging-launcher-chain for the exit-signal chain this repo already runs between Core and Launcher. WHY: an orphaned exec keeps consuming keystrokes from a console whose session ended long ago, and on 2026-08-20 this machine carried five orphaned core processes with the eldest alive 59 hours, so the failure is not hypothetical and its blast radius grows with uptime.

DECISION: ARTICLE 7 -- OUT-OF-CONSOLE REACH IS DEFENDED IN DEPTH, NOT BY A SINGLE CHECK. Touching a process outside the own console must be HARD, and it must be made hard by several independent layers so that one failing layer never opens the door alone. The layers, and each must be able to refuse by itself: a default-deny scope where in-console is the allowlist rather than out-of-console being a blocklist; an explicit named target, since a wildcard or a filter is not a name; a distinct, louder code path for out-of-console actions so such an action can never be reached by falling through an in-console one; a printed line naming the target and the layer that permitted it; and a caller-supplied justification for anything destructive. WHEN: designing or reviewing any exec, taskkill, injection, or query path that can name a process the caller did not spawn. HOW: run wkappbot skill read harness-guard-exemption-ladder-spec for the layered ladder this harness already uses, and treat every new out-of-console capability as requiring its own layer rather than reusing an existing one. WHY: the owner asked for safeguards in layers rather than a single gate, and the reason is visible in this very repo -- single-check protections have failed here repeatedly, from a guard that scanned only one family of tool names to a predicate that existed in two places and drifted, and in both cases one missing condition was the whole defence.

DECISION: ARTICLE 8 -- OWN CONSOLE FIRST, THEN OWN DESCENDANTS, AND THIS ORDERING BINDS THE INFORMATION COMMANDS TOO, TASKKILL ABOVE ALL. Every command that ACTS ON or REPORTS ON processes must rank candidates in this fixed order: processes attached to the own console first, then processes descended from the own console, then everything else last and only when explicitly named. WHEN: taskkill, tasklist, jobs, process queries, window enumeration, and any listing or classification a later decision will act upon. HOW: sort and scope by that order BEFORE any filter is applied, and run wkappbot skill read wktasklist-intelligent-management for the ranking and sanctuary rules already in force, together with wkappbot skill read wkappbot-taskkill-usage-howto for the kill-routing contract. WHY: the owner singled out taskkill because a kill is the least reversible act the toolchain can perform, and an information command is not innocent either -- a listing is the input to the next decision, so a listing that ranks a stranger first has already aimed the kill. This repo carries the evidence: a taskkill summary reported Killed N while every individual kill had been skipped by a safety guard, and a survey labelled five live Eye and screensaver daemons as orphaned zombies purely because their parent was null by design.

DECISION: ARTICLE 9 -- ADOPTION IS NOT BINDING, AND THE CLAIM IS PUBLISHED RATHER THAN GUESSED, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Article 3 forbids the working folder from SELECTING a partner, and that holds for BINDING, which means driving input into a console. ADOPTION is a different act on a different path: claiming control of a long-lived repo-scoped daemon that shares no console and no parent with the caller, the ordinary case being a daemon launched from a desktop shortcut. For adoption the repo IS the identity, because a daemon is defined by the repo it serves and not by whichever console happened to start it. THE MECHANISM IS MUTUAL AND MUST BE, because the reverse direction matters as much as the forward one: the daemon PUBLISHES its own claim at startup, writing repo root, pid, whether it holds a console, and start time into the repo state directory, and the session then READS that claim instead of scanning for a match. Adoption grants control verbs only, meaning status, stop, restart and query; it never grants the input side, which stays governed by Articles 2 through 4. WHEN: any command that must reach a daemon the caller did not spawn and shares no console with, and equally any daemon that must find the repo session it belongs to. HOW: read the published claim file rather than scanning by working directory, and run wkappbot skill read always-on-ai-automation-daemon-appbot-eye-internals for how a long-lived daemon here already records and exposes its own lifecycle state. WHY: the owner raised this case directly on 2026-08-20, and it is the one place where the working folder is genuinely the right identity rather than a stranger-selector -- but a CWD SCAN is still a guess while a published claim is a contract, which is the same reason this repo resolves session identity by exact file path instead of by scanning a shared working directory. Keeping adoption on its own louder path is also what Article 7 demands, since a control verb aimed outside the own console must never be reachable by falling through the in-console path.

DECISION: ARTICLE 10 -- THE DESKTOP IS A FENCE AND A CLASSIFIER, NEVER A SELECTOR. The owner observed on 2026-08-20 that a console window and a shortcut-launched daemon may well be children of the same desktop, and that is true, which is precisely why shared desktop ancestry must never be admitted as one of the Article 3 axes. The Windows shell is the ancestor of EVERY interactively launched process -- every console, every browser, every editor, and the daemon too -- so a rule satisfied by shared desktop ancestry is satisfied by the entire screen, and an axis that matches everything selects nothing. Admitting it as an OR axis is the wrong-window symptom written down as policy. THE TWO LEGITIMATE USES, and both are real. FIRST, AS A FENCE: the Windows session id and the window station, WinSta0 backslash Default, are genuine security boundaries, so reaching across a session, or from a session-0 service onto the interactive desktop, is forbidden outright -- this is a NECESSARY precondition and never a sufficient one, and it never counts toward the two agreeing axes. SECOND, AS A CLASSIFIER: a parent chain terminating at the shell is EVIDENCE THAT A HUMAN LAUNCHED THIS, which routes the process toward Article 9 adoption rather than Article 3 binding, and that routing decision is the useful half of the observation. WHEN: any resolution that is tempted to treat same-desktop, same-session or same-shell-ancestor as a match. HOW: apply it as a precondition and as a routing hint only, never as a candidate filter, and run wkappbot skill read concurrent-ai-isolation-env-var-detection-beats-parent-chain for why parent-chain evidence in this repo is read for what it CLASSIFIES rather than for what it selects. WHY: the general law under this Article is that the broader an identity signal is, the more it belongs at the boundary and the less it belongs in the choice -- CWD failed as a selector because a whole repo shares it, and desktop ancestry fails harder because a whole logon session shares it, yet both remain useful the moment they are demoted from choosing to bounding.

NAVIGATION: this core holds the ARTICLES, the law itself, and nothing else -- the evidence and the procedures live in two siblings so the law stays readable at load time. WHEN: you have read an Article and need either the proof behind it or the steps to apply it. HOW: for the incidents that produced each Article, meaning the agy input-corruption trace, the same-day correction of Article 5, the wkinject counter-example and the caller cascade as positive precedent, run wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution-ref; for the procedures, meaning the four-question review order, how to prove an input-side fix, how to decide binding versus adoption, and how to rank candidates in any listing or kill command, run wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution-howto. WHY: the first draft carried Articles, incidents and procedures in one flat skill and scored below the currency floor, which hard-blocked edits to the very file the constitution governs -- a law nobody can act on because it is too heavy to load is not a law, and the tier split is what keeps the Articles short enough to stay enforced.

DECISION: ARTICLE 13 -- THE OPERATING ENVIRONMENT IS A SHARED MULTI-TENANT DESKTOP, AND EVERY OTHER ARTICLE FOLLOWS FROM IT. The owner stated it plainly on 2026-08-20: at least FOUR intelligences run in parallel on his machine, they kill and interfere with each other, that produces bugs, and he then has to relaunch things himself. Any future reader who finds these Articles unnecessarily strict is reading them against the wrong machine -- there is no single-tenant desktop here to be relaxed for. WHAT THIS CHANGES, concretely. Consoles, window handles, process trees, the clipboard, the foreground window and the console input buffer are all SHARED resources with several live claimants at any moment, so a resolver that takes the first plausible match is not merely imprecise, it is statistically likely to select another agent's session. A kill aimed by a name or an image filter lands on a peer. And the damage is not confined to the tool that erred: the victim is a running conversation with unsaved context, which the owner must notice and restart by hand, so the cost is paid in his attention rather than in an error code. WHEN: reviewing any rule here and being tempted to loosen it, and whenever a resolver, a kill path, or an injector is being written or reviewed. HOW: assume at least three other agent sessions are live and ask what the code would select if the intended target were absent -- if the answer is anything other than nothing, it will eventually select a peer; run wkappbot skill read wktasklist-intelligent-management for the sanctuary rules that already encode this, and wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution-ref for the incidents. WHY: this is also why the global harness keeps an AI-work process set exempt from emergency reaping, why Article 7 demands layers rather than one gate, and why Article 8 orders even read-only listings -- each of those was written against the same fact, that the neighbours are not hypothetical.

DECISION: ARTICLE 8B -- A RESULT THAT BELONGS TO NOBODY IS EXCLUDED BY DEFAULT, NOT MERELY RANKED LAST. Owner directive 2026-08-27, and it sharpens Article 8 rather than repeating it: a search result matching NONE of this law's belonging tests -- not the caller-window fence, not the own console, not an own descendant -- must be moved OUT of the main result set into a separate OTHER MATCHES section printed at the very BOTTOM, one line per result, spending exactly ONE GRAP and ONE TITLE per line and nothing else -- the owner fixed this format on 2026-08-27, choosing it over outright exclusion. WHY THIS FORMAT AND NOT SUPPRESSION, and it is better than what this Article first proposed: a hidden result is a silent empty answer for anyone legitimately looking outside their console, while a bottom section keeps the finding DISCOVERABLE and still satisfies the Article 4 duty to name what was seen. It is nonetheless structurally stronger than a mere demotion, because the entries live in a SEPARATE SECTION rather than lower in the same list -- code that takes the first match of a filter, which is the failure Article 8 warns about, never reaches a section it does not parse, whereas a demoted row in the same list is still row N of that list. AND THE ONE-LINE BUDGET IS THE POINT OF THE FORMAT, not a cosmetic detail: a grap is copy-pasteable and therefore ACTIONABLE on its own, so one grap plus one title is the minimum that lets a human act deliberately on a foreign window, while spending no tree, no rect, no pattern list and no node dump on something that does not belong to the caller. The cost of a stranger appearing is thus capped at one line, which is what makes it safe to keep showing them. WHEN: any listing, search, enumeration or classification a later decision will act upon -- a11y find, a11y windows, window enumeration, process queries, tasklist, jobs. HOW: run wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution-howto for the candidate-ranking procedure, then implement FOUR TIERS and let the existing keyboard, mouse and foreground priority act as a TIE-BREAKER WITHIN a tier and never across tiers: T0 attached to the caller own console, T1 descended from it, T2 passes a fence such as the same window station or Windows session but belongs to none of the above, T3 matches no belonging axis at all and is suppressed. WHY THIS IS STRONGER THAN A BETTER SORT KEY, which is the whole point of the owner phrasing it as exclusion: Article 8 already warns that a listing is the INPUT to the next decision, so a stranger that is merely demoted is still selectable by anything taking the first match of a filter -- demotion improves what a human reads while leaving what a program picks unchanged. Exclusion is Article 7 default-deny applied to output, where in-console is the ALLOWLIST rather than out-of-console being a blocklist. TWO REQUIREMENTS ON THE EXCLUSION, both load-bearing. FIRST, IT MUST NEVER BE SILENT: a suppressed set still prints its count and the flag that would reveal it, because Article 4 requires a line naming what was seen and why it was refused, and a caller legitimately searching for a window outside its console must get an explanation rather than an empty list -- a silent empty result is a worse failure than the one being fixed. SECOND, AN EXPLICIT hwnd OR pid IN THE GRAP IS ITSELF THE EXPLICIT NAMING Article 8 permits, so suppression must never apply to a handle the caller named outright; the code must distinguish caller-named from pattern-matched. AND THE CARVE-OUT THAT MUST SURVIVE: Article 9 adoption is a DIFFERENT act on a different path, reaching a daemon that shares no console by its published claim, so if a search path is what adoption uses, blanket exclusion would break it -- the exclusion belongs to the BINDING path, not the adoption path. MEASURED PROVOCATION, first-hand 2026-08-27: WindowFinder.cs line 664 ranks candidates keyboard 3, mouse 2, foreground 1, other 0, and line 2284 sorts on it. Every one of those axes is desktop-GLOBAL, there is no own-console tier anywhere in the ranking, and the sort runs AFTER the filter loop rather than before it as Article 8 requires -- so on this four-session desktop the ranking can and does put a peer first, which is exactly what Article 14 recorded when a live a11y find showed the focus sitting on another AI session window sharing the same terminal process.

DECISION: ARTICLE 8B IS A RENDERING RULE PLUS AN ORDERING RULE, AND SEPARATING THE TWO DISSOLVES ITS BLAST RADIUS. An audit of the a11y search path on 2026-08-27 reported HIGH RISK on three callers -- Chrome and CDP placement, Article 9 daemon adoption, and pattern-only find -- on the assumption that non-belonging results would be dropped from the RESULT SET. That assumption is what creates the risk, and it is not what the owner asked for. WHEN: implementing the OTHER MATCHES section, or reviewing any objection that it would break an existing caller. HOW: run wkappbot skill read exec-console-binding-constitution-howto, then split the change in two -- the LIST that FindWindows returns stays COMPLETE and loses nothing, while the RENDERER prints it in two sections, belonging results in full above and everything else one grap-plus-title line at the bottom; separately, the list is ORDERED by tier so T0 and T1 sort ahead of T2 and T3 with keyboard, mouse and foreground demoted to a within-tier tie-break. WHY THE SPLIT MATTERS: a programmatic caller consumes the returned LIST and never parses the printed text, so a sectioned output cannot break Chrome placement or daemon adoption -- nothing was removed for them to miss. What those callers ARE sensitive to is which element sits at index zero, and that is fixed by the ORDERING half, in their favour, since a caller taking the first match currently gets whichever window happened to hold keyboard focus. So the two halves answer two different failures: ordering fixes what a PROGRAM picks, sectioning fixes what a HUMAN reads and what a listing COSTS. AND THE THIRD THING SECTIONING DOES, which the owner named on 2026-08-27 and which is the reason showing strangers at all is defensible: A CLEAR LABEL TRANSFERS RESPONSIBILITY. Once the output has stated plainly that these results do not belong to the caller, anyone who reaches for one anyway has made a deliberate choice, and the consequence is theirs rather than the tool having mis-aimed them. That is what lets this Article show foreign windows instead of hiding them -- hiding would protect the tool while blinding the operator, whereas labelling protects both. IT FOLLOWS THAT THE LABEL MUST BE UNMISTAKABLE, and this is a hard requirement rather than a style note: responsibility only moves if the warning is impossible to miss, so the section needs a header that says outright that these do not belong to this console, not a dim colour, not a one-character marker, and not a term a reader could take for a mere relevance ranking. A subtle label leaves the tool holding the blame it thought it had handed over. AND THE DIRECTION OF BLAME BEFORE THE FIX LANDS, which the owner named on 2026-08-27 and which this Article owed a sentence to: while the listing is still mis-ordered and unlabelled, it is UNFAIR to fault the intelligence for picking the wrong window out of it. Article 8 already says a listing that ranks a stranger first has ALREADY AIMED the kill; the missing corollary is that the hand which aimed it is the TOOL's, not the reader's. A session handed four indistinguishable matches, ordered by whichever tab happened to hold keyboard focus that second, has been set up to fail and then blamed for failing -- and it cannot even detect the problem, because nothing in that output says which result is its own. THE PRACTICAL RULE THIS CREATES, in both directions. BEFORE the tier ordering and the label ship, any guard, skill, or review that scolds a session for acting on a foreign window is punishing a TOOL defect through the model, so the correct response to such an incident is to fix the listing rather than to add a rule telling sessions to be more careful -- a caution cannot be obeyed against information the reader was never given. AFTER they ship, the same incident reads oppositely: the output stated plainly that the result did not belong, so acting on it anyway is a deliberate choice and the consequence is the actor's. THE GENERAL LAW worth carrying beyond this file: responsibility follows INFORMATION. You may hold an agent to a rule only once the interface has told it what it needs to obey that rule, so whenever an agent keeps making the same wrong choice, look first at whether the tool made the right choice VISIBLE -- an instruction added on top of an unreadable interface is a rule written where nobody can read it. THE LIVE INSTANCE, found in this repo the same day and worth fixing as part of Article 8B rather than separately: CommandHelp.Entries.A11y.cs line 126 documents the ambiguity marker as 'N matches found -- tighten grap using score hints'. That message hands the disambiguation homework to the caller, and on the measured run it printed AMB:4 when THREE of those four matches were other sessions windows. No amount of pattern-tightening can fix that, because a caller cannot know a peer tab title in advance and has no business guessing at one -- the strangers should never have been in the ambiguous set to begin with. It is the blame-direction defect in a single line of help text. THE FIX FALLS OUT OF THE TIERS AT NO EXTRA COST, and it improves the guard rather than merely softening it: once T2 and T3 results move to the OTHER MATCHES section, only belonging candidates count toward ambiguity, so that same run reports AMB:1 instead of AMB:4. The ambiguity guard becomes MORE accurate, not less strict -- what disappears is FALSE ambiguity manufactured by peer pollution, which is the kind that trains a reader to ignore the marker. Update the help text alongside the ordering so it stops prescribing a remedy the caller cannot perform. This is the same standard Article 4 sets for a refusal, which must print one line naming which article failed and what it saw -- an unreadable refusal is not a refusal, and an unreadable label is not a label. MEASURED FIRST-HAND the same day, which is why the cost half is not cosmetic: a11y find on a four-tab terminal returned four matches, three of them peers -- another session, a different repo session, and a daemon -- and each stranger consumed about fourteen lines including a full System block of memory and handle counts and a full Mouse block, both repeated verbatim per match. The owner one-line budget turns roughly forty-two lines of stranger into three. The own window ranked first only because it happened to hold focus at that instant; switching tabs would have put the other repo session at index zero. The ambiguity guard also fired AMB:4 on that run, so peer pollution is inflating false ambiguity as well. THE ONE PLACE A CARVE-OUT IS STILL REQUIRED, and the audit found the gate already exists: WindowFinder distinguishes an explicit hwnd filter from a pattern search, so a handle the caller named outright is the explicit naming Article 8 permits and must never be sectioned away.

ARTICLE 16, OWNER DIRECTIVE 2026-09-07, AND IT SUPPLIES THE ONE THING 8C LACKED -- A SANCTIONED WAY THROUGH. Reaching another console's property is permitted ONLY behind a CONFESSIONAL LONG OPTION, and this binds EVERY a11y ACTION as well as taskkill: his words were that touching another console's property must be allowed only when the scary option is attached, and that this covers all the a11y actions and taskkill too. SCOPE: a11y click, type, invoke, read, screenshot, window move or close, taskkill, and every CDP verb that drives a page -- anything acting on a window, element, process or tab outside T0-T1. THE FORM: --i-really-want-to-meddle-with-another-caller-app=<number>. THREE PROPERTIES ARE DELIBERATE AND MUST SURVIVE ANY REDESIGN. It carries NO wk PREFIX, because a wk name reads as a sanctioned tool and this is not a tool, it is a CONFESSION -- the owner said so explicitly. It is long and ugly ON PURPOSE so it cannot be typed by reflex or reached by falling through an ordinary path, which is Article 7's louder-separate-path layer made concrete. And it TAKES AN ARGUMENT, so the flag alone is insufficient and the caller must name WHICH target it means, which is Article 7's explicit-named-target layer. WHY THIS IS CONSTITUTIONAL: a default-deny with no sanctioned way through becomes a wall that sessions route around, the guard-blocks-its-own-remedy class this repo has measured repeatedly -- the confession IS the way through, and its cost is paid in deliberateness rather than friction. AND THE ACCEPTANCE TEST IS THE OWNER'S, given the same day: separation is not done when the LEDGER knows, it is done when a11y find SHOWS it. Measured 2026-09-07, it does not yet -- a11y find listed four Chrome windows as this console's own while the ledger assigned one of them to a different caller, so Article 8B's two-section rendering is the VISIBLE half of this law and must be keyed to the ownership ledger rather than to process identity alone. DECISION: ARTICLE 8C -- TASKKILL AND TASKLIST TAKE THE SAME TIERS AS THE SEARCH PATH, BUT A KILL DEFAULT-DENIES WHERE A LISTING ONLY SECTIONS. Owner directive 2026-08-27, extending Article 8B from window search to the process commands Article 8 already named. WHEN: any change to taskkill, tasklist, jobs, or process classification, and before trusting any of their output. HOW: run wkappbot skill read wkappbot-taskkill-usage-howto for the kill-routing contract and wkappbot skill read wktasklist-intelligent-management for the ranking and sanctuary rules, then apply the SAME T0-T3 belonging computation as Article 8B, with treatments that differ by REVERSIBILITY: a LISTING may show a foreign entry once it is clearly labelled and sectioned, because a label transfers responsibility; a KILL may not, because no label makes an irreversible act safe, so T2 and T3 must be DEFAULT-DENIED and reachable only by the explicit naming Article 8 permits, on the louder separate path Article 7 demands. MEASURED FIRST-HAND 2026-08-27, and the shape is worse than expected. TaskkillCompatCommand.Classify.cs ClassifyOne at line 149 decides PROTECTED, ZOMBIE or UNKNOWN through five stages, and EVERY protective axis is a NAME or TOKEN match: image equals claude, codex or gemini returns PROTECTED, and a hardcoded token list -- eye, wkchat, mcp, whisper-ring, screensaver, agent, claude -- returns PROTECTED when found anywhere in the command line. There is NO ownership test in the function at all. Consequently a PEER session's helper process, a python or node or dotnet child carrying none of those tokens, cannot reach the protected class on any path. This is precisely the failure Article 13 names, that a kill aimed by a name or an image filter lands on a peer, and it is the exact INVERSION of the shape Article 7 requires, since the protection is an allowlist of NAMES while ownership -- the thing that actually decides whether a process is yours -- never enters the decision. A SECOND DEFECT IN THE SAME FUNCTION: stage one classifies an EMPTY COMMAND LINE as ZOMBIE, the auto-reap class, with no ownership test either. That is the mechanism behind the incident already recorded in this constitution, where a survey labelled five live Eye and screensaver daemons as orphaned zombies purely because their parent was null by design -- and a command-line read can also come back empty from a permission or timing failure on a perfectly healthy peer process, so the rule reaps on ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE. THE FIX IS THE SAME TIER COMPUTATION, WIRED AHEAD OF THE NAME STAGES: resolve the tier first, let T0 and T1 proceed to the existing classification, and refuse T2 and T3 outright unless the caller named the pid explicitly and supplied the justification Article 7 requires for anything destructive. Ownership must be the FIRST question rather than an absent one, and the name list then does what it is good at -- protecting your OWN long-lived daemons from your OWN reaper -- instead of standing in for a boundary it was never able to draw.

DECISION: ARTICLE 15 -- a browser window belongs to the CALLER WINDOW that asked for it, and a different caller window gets a NEW INSTANCE rather than a share of the old one. Owner ruling 2026-09-02. WHEN: any code deciding whether to reuse a running Chrome or launch a fresh one, any code answering is this browser window mine, and any placement decision that moves a browser window. HOW: run wkappbot skill read cdp-open-reuse-existing-chrome-tab for the ownership ledger this article governs and wkappbot skill read standard-appbot-window for how a caller window is resolved, then key BOTH the reuse probe and the ledger on the caller window -- never on the working folder, never on a project hash, never on the port -- and when the resolved caller window does not match the recorded owner, LAUNCH A NEW INSTANCE instead of attaching; the split and the refusal must each print one line naming the caller window seen and the owner found, which is the duty Article 4 already sets for every refusal in this law. WHY: this is constitutional rather than a preference, because Article 1 says the console IS the identity and Article 3 forbids the working folder from SELECTING a partner, and a browser window driven by CDP is a partner in exactly that sense since input goes into it -- so binding it by folder was already outside this law while the ledger did it anyway, and Article 7 default-deny supplies the rest, an unowned browser window is refused and never adopted by a fallback because a gate that cannot answer NO is not a gate. WHAT THIS ARTICLE DOES NOT DECIDE, and the next session must MEASURE rather than derive: how a caller window resolves per host, since VS Code hosts many terminals in ONE window while Windows Terminal gives per-tab handles under one shared pid, so a bare handle merges the first and splits the second; and what becomes of a window a PREDECESSOR opened, since the folder key existed precisely so a successor could inherit it and a window key orphans it at handoff -- Article 9 adoption by published claim is the likeliest shape for that second answer, but it is a lead and not yet law.
